desc:
Each meeting is a half-open range [start, end). After a meeting ends, its room needs cleaning units of time before anybody may use it again, so a room that hosted a meeting ending at time e can host another meeting that starts at time e + cleaning or later. A room is also clean at the start of the day.

Return the minimum number of rooms needed to hold all the meetings.

meetings = [[1, 4], [4, 6], [6, 9]], cleaning = 0  ->  1
meetings = [[1, 4], [4, 6], [6, 9]], cleaning = 1  ->  2
meetings = [[1, 4], [4, 6], [6, 9]], cleaning = 3  ->  3
constraints: The meetings are in no particular order
hints: Without cleaning time this is the classic minimum-rooms problem. What changes when a room stays blocked a little longer?
A meeting effectively occupies its room during [start, end + cleaning).
The answer is the largest number of these extended ranges that cover one moment. Sort starts and extended ends separately and sweep, or use a min-heap of room-free times.
editorial: Replace each meeting by the extended range [start, end + cleaning): during it the room cannot be given to anyone else. Two meetings can share a room exactly when their extended ranges do not overlap, so the question is the maximum number of extended ranges covering a common moment (interval graphs can always be coloured with as many colours as the maximum clique).

Implementation with a min-heap of the times at which rooms become usable: process meetings by start; if the earliest-free room is usable at or before the start, pop it (reuse); push end + cleaning for the current meeting. The heap size at the end is the number of rooms. Equivalent two-pointer version: sort the starts and sort the extended ends; for every start, if it is at least the smallest unused extended end, advance that end pointer (reuse), otherwise count a new room. Time O(n log n), space O(n). Note that end + cleaning can reach 2·109, which overflows a 32-bit signed integer, so use 64-bit arithmetic in such languages.
